result.topic_en: Euler concludes that a power whose exponent shares a divisor with Q = P−1 cannot give a primitive root, proves in Corollary 4 that the 'socius' (associated residue) of a primitive root is also a primitive root, and announces a table of primitive roots for small primes.

Q communem habeat diuiſorem, qui ſit $d$, vt tam
$\frac{Q}{d}$ quam $\frac{m}{d}$ ſit numerus integer; in progreſſione
geometrica $1, a^{m}, a^{2m}, a^{3m}, a^{4m}$ occurret pote-
ſtas, cuius ſcilicet exponens $=\frac{Q}{d}m$, antequam ad

que multiplum ipſius Q, ex ea poteſtate iam orie-
tur reſiduum 1, ac propterea ſeries reſiduorum pro-
dibit incompleta. Talis ergo poteſtas $a^{m}$ ſeu reſi-
duum inde reſultans certe non erit radix primitiua.

Coroll. 4.

49. Si reſiduum $r$ praebeat radicem primiti-
vam, etiam eius ſocium $s$ dabit radicem primiti-
vam. Poſito enim diuiſore primo $P=2n+1$ vt
ſit $Q=2n$, ſit $a^{n-\lambda}$ poteſtas praebens reſiduum $r$,
et ſocium $s$ reſultat ex poteſtate $a^{n+\lambda}$. Euidens
autem eſt ſi $n-\lambda$ fuerit ad $Q=2n$ primus, tum
etiam exponentem alterum $n+\lambda$ fore ad Q primum.

Scholion.

50. Haud abs re fore arbitror, ſi pro ſimpli-
cioribus diuiſoribus primis P tam numeros ad $Q=P-1$
primos, quam radices primitiuas iis reſpondentes
conſpectui expoſuero:

O 2 Diui-

items.quote: Talis ergo poteſtas $a^{m}$ ſeu reſiduum inde reſultans certe non erit radix primitiua.
items.english: Therefore such a power $a^m$, or the residue resulting from it, will certainly not be a primitive root.

items.quote: Si reſiduum $r$ praebeat radicem primitivam, etiam eius ſocium $s$ dabit radicem primitivam.
items.english: If the residue $r$ yields a primitive root, its associate $s$ will also yield a primitive root.

items.quote: Haud abs re fore arbitror, ſi pro ſimplicioribus diuiſoribus primis P tam numeros ad $Q=P-1$ primos, quam radices primitiuas iis reſpondentes conſpectui expoſuero:
